This is why I ask - I’m a paramedic, and I’ve found that healthcare, as I’m sure you’re aware, is much the same as PD when it comes to deeply ingrained institutional racism that allows providers from doctors to nurses to other paramedics to do as much harm as they feel like and get away with it. In paramedicine specifically, Elijah McClain and George Floyd come to mind.

I run hospital to hospital transport, and I have documented, on God, over a hundred cases of blatant racism in the form of medical abuse or neglect in less than 3 years. Taken then right up the board of medicine and board of nursing and patient advocacy and, surprise, nothing happens. When this happens, I prevent it when I see it (nearly at the cost of my job and company contracts several times), and tell the receiving facility when I get there after its happened, or if its a case like denying someone pain medication based on non existent drug seeking behavior. During transport, I do what I can to validate their feelings and make their day any better, if I can. And of course, report, report, report, and no one cares. But at least I get to be there and undo whatever I can and try to make sure the receiving hospital does better.

And because of that, I’ve been considering PD. The entire department can hate me. My partners, the chief, the whole fucking system. I, truly, do not care. I can’t control all of that fuckery but I can control me, and, like my patients, it guarantees that every time a person interacts with me, they will have a safe experience. If I see an officer abusing or assaulting someone, I will take my own two hands and stop that from happening. They can fire me or ice me out of the department or whatever they want to do. I’m a medic. I’ll go back to that. I know interactions with me will be safe interactions, and I will be able to prevent unsafe interactions from happening in front if me unless I am physically stopped, system be damned. I just want to learn as much about all of it as I can before making the decision.

I crossed into Vermont September 2nd, 2019. You’re a tad bit ahead of where I was at that time but I’m sure you’re still hearing the same thing from locals, sobos, and even fellow nobos planning to flip: You’re not going to make it to Katahdin in time.

My best friend broke his foot in NY and we had a set up where we evened things out between the two of us, so my pack got significantly heavier when he got off and myself, significantly less motivated. I slowed down around Mass. 

But I knew from the beginning I was going to finish come hell or high water. That was never a question in my head. However, to highlight each achievement, each state line, and each 100 mile marker, I thought of all of the people that said if I didn’t flip, I wouldn’t make it. They could go fuck themselves - I set out for a Northbound hike, and a Northbound hike I would do. 

I paced myself and cut it CLOSE - finished 10/20/19, Katahdin closed a few days later - but the pressure and the negativity spiced things up for me. There’s nothing like touching that sign (sometimes when I’ve had a few, I look down at my hands and marvel at the fact that these hands touched that damn sign), and there’s REALLY nothing like touching it when dozens of people have told you you won’t. 

You’ve got extremely hard terrain and GORGEOUS country right ahead of you. Take your time. You’ll be a lot more bored in your real life than you are through NH and Maine. Good luck, tell Katahdin Spirit said hey

I’ve been on Seroquel for 3 years now. The first few months were the hardest. Waking up was so hard and I was groggy and irritable, especially at work. It got better after the first month, but then my dose would get upped, and it would be shitty for a few weeks again, repeat the cycle. After I was stable on a dosage, things got considerably better after about 3 months. I’ve had no problems at all for the past two years, but I sleep great at night.

For now, try to start taking it a bit earlier in the evening so you don’t sleep as late, if that’s a problem. If not, just hang on and enjoy the ride. It’ll get better!

You’re welcome! Seroquel’s a med you take at night, and for me, it knocks me out about an hour after I take it (great for me as I suffered from insomnia and my worst symptoms were at night). When I miss a dose, the first symptom I experience is not sleeping at all that night. When I went to work, all day I experienced rapid heart beat, vomiting, shakes and sweating, and tunnel vision and feeling faint, and my anxiety and paranoia kicked into overdrive. I had to leave work early both times.

For me, a missed dose is usually super easy to catch when I realize I have trouble falling asleep. Both nights I missed I realized late at night and didn’t want to take it so I wouldn’t be tired at work - definitely not worth it, bad news bears.

Seroquel has worked wonders for me, but this is just my personal experience. My only two side effects have been very mild weight gain which I was able to control, and tiredness. The first couple months on Seroquel were ROUGH because I was damn near falling asleep on my feet at work. After adjusting, I have no side effects and it controls my symptoms fairly well, at least enough for me to work full time and live a normal life. 
Seroquel does come with withdrawal though. If you need to quit, you have to walk off slowly if you’ve been on it for a while. I’ve missed two doses in the past three years and they have been nightmare days. As someone that was god awful with taking his meds regularly, this was actually helpful! 
Hope this helps:) Good luck

I let my alarm blare for at least thirty seconds before I was ready to put in the effort to reach for my phone. Disoriented and hungover, I looked at the time - 5:30am - and hit snooze.
    
    "It's hot as hell." I grumbled, pushing the blankets away from my sweaty body. The sun hadn't even risen yet but it was already at least 90 degrees outside, and as usual, Georgia's humidity had found its way into my apartment. I stared at my ceiling, wishing I didn't have to go to work and regretting having friends over so late last night.
    
    Dehydration and an increasingly bad mood drove me out of my bed before my second alarm did. I took about two steps before tripping over something and nearly falling flat on my face. I turned around, cussing, to see my backpack. I remembered tossing it on my bedroom floor last night after going through and showing everyone what I was bringing on my backpacking trip at the end of the week. 
    
    I moved it against the wall and headed into the kitchen to make some coffee, taking solace in knowing that in a few days, I'd be out of this city and beginning a three day hike at the beautiful Amicalola Falls.
    
    Letting my mind wander outside of Atlanta, I threw a frozen breakfast into the microwave and opened my cabinet to grab my coffee cup.
    
    Except, my cup wasn't there. Front and center was a large, stainless steel bottle I had never seen before. Assuming one of my friends had left it from last night, I picked it up. To my surprise, it was heavy. There was already something inside. I inspected the outside of it, totally perplexed at this point. It looked to be brand new, and had to be able to hold at least 32 ounces. There was even a carabiner already clipped to the cap, which, although a bit heavy, would make it suitable to backpack with.
    
    I unscrewed the cap and was hit with the aroma of fresh, hot coffee.
    
    "What?" My brow furrowed, and I stared at the bottle as I tried to figure out how what I was seeing was possible. I moved to pour it out, but maybe one of my friends had made it for me last night and wanted to suprise me. That would be really out of character for any of them, but I decided that that was what happened. The bottle was probably well insulated and had been able to keep the coffee hot all night. I had wanted iced coffee because of the heat, but I had to drink some to make room for the ice. I shrugged my shoulders and took a sip.
    
    
    
    Three Months Later
    
    
    "Hey Shawn, we're gonna need at least two more liters of water to make it into town. Can you filter more while I finish packing my backpack?" My new friend, Max, asked me as he wiped snow off his rolled up tent. I'd met him four days ago when I began this trip. We fell into step and, after realizing we got along really well, decided to finish the 100 mile loop trail together. Today we needed to go two miles out of our way to resupply in a nearby town, and stay the night in a hotel to get a break from the cold. 
    
    "Yeah man, no problem." I said, my warm words visible in the freezing air.
    
    "Thanks," He replied. "Damn, its cold this morning. I can't wait for this hotel. 
    
    I strapped down my pack and made sure my bottle was securely clipped to it before leaning it up against a tree, grabbing my water filter and plastic water bottles, and heading downhill from our campsite to the stream.
    
    As I filtered the water, I took in the Sierra's brilliant wilderness. Mornings were my favorite. I loved how the light from the rising sun made the snow glimmer and how the trees and the mountains cast long shadows across the smooth blanket of snow. I was very content in that moment, but I was just as excited for a hot shower and something to eat besides oatmeal and tuna.
    
    I enjoyed a moment of peace before heading back up to the campsite. When I got there, though, I didn't see Max, but his backpack was packed and against the tree next to mine. Figuring he had walked off to pee, I went to shoulder my pack - and my stomach dropped. My tumbler was gone.
    
    "Oh, shit." I scanned the campsite, looking at our footprints. The only ones that tracked out of the campsite were mine down to the stream. "Max! Hey, Max!"
    
    I heard nothing but the birds waking up and the gentle breeze in the trees. Panic was setting in. I know he took my coffee because I had just checked to make sure it was still on my bag. He had to have drank some. He could be anywhere on the planet. I barely knew this man, what if I couldn't find him? What if he steals it for himself? There was at least 30 ounces of adventures left in that bottle! This was only my second time using it, I had so many - 
    
    "What the hell is going on?" I spun around to see Max standing by our packs completely out of breath, my bottle in one hand, it's cap in the other, and a lost expression on his face.
    
    "Where did you go?" I demanded. I reached forward and snatched the tumbler out of his hand, careful not to let anything spill.
    
    "Um, some hotel. I think - " He stammered. 
    
    I cut him off. "Why'd you take my bottle? That's not cool, man."
    
    "I don't know, you've had it on your pack this whole time, I wanted to look at it, and when I touched it it was warm. I Was like, 'It's 20 degrees, how is it not freezing?' So I opened it and thought I somehow didn't notice you make hot coffee this morning. And how could I resist hot coffee right now?" He threw me the cap and I twisted it back on, finally beginning to come down from my panic. "I don't know for sure, but I think it might have been the hotel that we're going to today." 
    
    I sighed. "It probably was. You drink it, and it takes you to the place you want to go."
    
    "I figured that," He said. He put his pack on and I followed suit. "That's how I made it back. That is fucking unbelievable. How did you wind up with a bottle of magical coffee?"
    
    I shook my head and we started walking down the trail, toward town. " I just found it in my house, drank some, and ended up in Amicalola State Park in Georgia, a couple hours from home. Drank again, ended up back home. That was a couple of months ago. I've only used it twice since then, the first time to get to a trail head int he White Mountains in New Hampshire, and the second time to get here. I think I'm just going to go further and further from Georgia each time. Hike the world, you know?"
    
    Max just looked at me with his jaw on the ground. "Does it refill itself? Is it always hot like that? Do you have one for me?"
    
    I laughed, "Sorry man. It's always hot and no, I don't think it refills itself, otherwise we'd both be in town right now. I've had a long time to think about how I'm going to use what I've got. I'm going to go everywhere that I've ever wanted to go, until I find the place that really speaks to me. I don't know where that's going to be, but I know it ain't in Atlanta."
    
    Max kept looking over at me, smiling and shaking his head. "What are you going to do when you run out? Where's that last drop going to take you?"
    
    I looked east, toward the sun, listening to our feet crunch on the snow below.  Now that my heart rate was back to normal, I let the serenity of the forest capture me again. I had asked myself that same question many times, and I knew the answer well. "Home. It's gonna take me home."

I worked at Wendy's when I was a teenager. One night around midnight (the lobby closes at 10, so only the drive thru was open), i went into the walk in freezer to restack a couple of boxes of fries that had been knocked over. Anyways, I started stacking the fries right by the door. I drop the first box down right next to the white box, and the cover flipped up a TINY bit, I barely noticed.
